paragraphs.heading: What it means
paragraphs.text: Independence is a basic idea in probability, in statistics and in the theory of stochastic processes. Two events are independent when one of them happening does not change the probability that the other happens, or, saying the same thing another way, does not change its odds. In the same spirit, two random variables are independent when the value one takes leaves the probability distribution of the other unchanged. When one event does shift the chances of another, the events are called dependent.

paragraphs.heading: Dice and cards
paragraphs.text: Roll a die twice: getting a 6 the first time and getting a 6 the second time are independent events. But a 6 on the first roll and a total of 8 across both rolls are not independent. Draw two cards from a deck, putting the first back before drawing again, and a red card on each draw are independent events. Without putting it back they are dependent, since a deck missing one red card has a smaller share of red cards left.

paragraphs.heading: It runs both ways
paragraphs.text: If A is independent of B, then B is also independent of A: the occurrence of either one leaves the probability of the other alone. Some ways of writing the definition use conditional probabilities. They can look more natural, but they are not the preferred form, because they can be undefined when P(A) or P(B) is 0. The preferred definition also makes the two-way symmetry obvious.

paragraphs.heading: More than two events
paragraphs.text: With three or more events, two kinds of independence have to be kept apart. Events are pairwise independent when every pair of them is independent. They are mutually independent when each event is independent of any combination of the others. Mutual independence brings pairwise independence with it, but pairwise independence alone does not guarantee the mutual kind. When people say independent without saying which, they usually mean mutual.

paragraphs.heading: Checking every combination
paragraphs.text: Mutual independence is more than one condition multiplying together the probabilities of all the single events. It has to hold for every subset of the events too. A set of three events can even have no pair that is independent, which rules out mutual independence for the whole set.

paragraphs.heading: Odd corners
paragraphs.text: An event is independent of itself only if it almost surely happens or almost surely does not; this fact is handy when proving zero–one laws. Likewise, a random variable is independent of itself only if it is almost surely constant. A covariance of 0 does not settle the question, because two random variables with zero covariance may still be dependent. Finally, X and Y are conditionally independent given Z when, once Z is known, learning Y tells you nothing more about X.
